target_customer: Rental brokers, brokerages, landlords and property managers
problem: Rental brokers had to enter and syndicate listings across many sites by hand; the founders built broker-tested listing management software after working as brokers.
business_model: SaaS subscription per user (50 dollars a month for one user in 2011) with leads and applications
product_category: Rental listing management and apartment marketing software

founders.name: Gordon Chen
prior_employers: Boston rental brokerage (worked as a broker for a year)
founders.background_notes: TechCrunch March 2011 says he and his co-founder are engineers who worked a year as brokers in Boston.

founders.name: Yanjun (Yan) Li
prior_employers: Boston rental brokerage (worked as a broker for a year)
founders.background_notes: The YC page lists Yanjun (Yan) Li; TechCrunch 2011 calls the co-founder John Li, so the name differs between sources.

competitors.name: RentJuice
competitors.what: Rental listing management and syndication software for brokers
competitors.funding_then: Had just raised 6.2 million dollars and acquired Kahoots

technical_complexity.rationale: Listing management, syndication feeds and mobile apps are standard web work; the hard part is local broker relationships and data feeds.

defensibility.rationale: Brokers' listing data and workflows create modest lock in, but a funded rival already sold the same product.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: No acquisition by an incumbent was found; the company expanded into leads, applications and leases and is still operating in 2026.

market_need_then: In March 2011 TechCrunch reported the company claimed about 75 percent of the Boston market and about 10 percent of Chicago, with landlords able to distribute listings free and brokers paying 50 to 100 dollars a month.

brand_strength.rationale: A long descriptive phrase name with no sources showing press, merch or community about the brand.

outcome_analysis: You Got Listings was bootstrapped by two engineers who worked as brokers, raised 150,000 dollars from the Start Fund and claimed strong share in Boston and Chicago in 2011. It stayed small, with a listed team of 3, and now sells an all in one rental platform covering leads, applications and leases. No later venture funding or exit was found.
notes: The 20K seed with Y Combinator rests on a single database (CB Insights) and its date is unknown; the 150K Start Fund figure comes from TechCrunch. YC lists founded 2009. The about page returned 503. Funding history is thin, so coverage is partial. Only one dated competitor is listed because the New York rental sites (StreetEasy, Naked Apartments) found in search targeted different users and were not tied to the company.
